title: The Theory of Two Truths in India

summaries.example: Imagine a clay pot. In everyday life, we call it a pot, fill it with water, and use it. But if we break it into pieces, the single pot is no longer there. Some Buddhist thinkers called the pot conventionally real: it is real for ordinary life, but it depends on its parts and on the name we give it. Other thinkers asked whether even the smallest parts could stand on their own.
summaries.summary: The theory of two truths is a long-running discussion in Indian Buddhist philosophy. It distinguishes conventional truth, which concerns ordinary ways of speaking and understanding, from ultimate truth, which concerns what careful investigation reveals. The distinction did not have just one meaning. Sarvāstivāda thinkers treated ordinary objects such as pots as made from more basic atoms and moments. Sautrāntika thinkers emphasized momentary, causally effective particulars and treated general ideas as conceptual. Yogācāra thinkers argued that what we experience conventionally consists of mental representations rather than independently existing outside objects. Madhyamaka thinkers went further: they argued that things are empty of an independent essence. For them, emptiness does not mean that nothing exists. It means that things arise dependently. The discussion also includes the idea that emptiness itself is not a new permanent foundation. The two truths matter because Buddhist thinkers connected correct understanding with the possibility of nirvāṇa, or freedom from suffering.
key_ideas: Many Indian Buddhist thinkers used two kinds of truth to explain how things appear in everyday life and how they are understood through deeper investigation.
Different Buddhist schools gave very different meanings to conventional and ultimate truth.
Some schools said basic atoms, moments of consciousness, or mental experiences were ultimately real.
Madhyamaka thinkers argued that nothing has a completely independent essence, including emptiness itself.
Understanding these ideas was connected with the Buddhist goal of freedom from suffering.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that one religious and philosophical tradition can contain several serious answers to the same question. It also teaches a careful lesson about perspective: everyday language can help us live and communicate, while deeper analysis can show how dependent and changeable things are. The debate asks whether freedom from suffering requires changing what we know, how we see ourselves, or both.

important_terms.definition: A way things are understood in ordinary life, through everyday names, ideas, and practices.
A deeper way of examining reality, beyond ordinary names and ideas.
The idea that things do not have a completely independent, unchanging essence.
The idea that things arise because they depend on causes, conditions, parts, and names.
A Buddhist term for freedom from suffering and the troubles caused by craving and other afflictions.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be useful in everyday life even if it depends on many parts?
Is a name like “pot” part of the thing, or is it something people add?
Why might a philosopher say that even a deeper truth should not become a fixed object?
How could seeing things as dependent change the way someone lives?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “A person made a promise.” In ordinary conversation, it is meaningful to identify a person as the agent of the promise. Candrakīrti’s Madhyamaka analysis does not simply erase that person. Instead, it asks whether the person can be found as something independent of the five aggregates—body, feelings, perceptions, dispositions, and consciousness. It argues that no independent self is found, while a person can still function as a conventional designation dependent on those aggregates. This illustrates how conventional usefulness and ultimate analysis can coexist without making the person intrinsically real.
summaries.summary: The Indian Buddhist theory of two truths distinguishes conventional truth from ultimate truth, but the distinction was interpreted in competing ways. The entry presents the development from an early interpretive contrast into detailed ontological, epistemological, and semantic theories. In the Sarvāstivāda or Vaibhāṣika account, composite objects and temporal continuities are conventionally real, whereas atoms, point-instant consciousnesses, and other irreducible units are ultimately real. Sautrāntika replaces this picture with an epistemological distinction: momentary unique particulars are directly perceived and causally efficient, while universals are conceptual and inferential. Yogācāra denies the conventional reality of external physical objects, explaining experience through mental representations and latent impressions. Madhyamaka challenges all such foundations. In its Svātantrika forms, conventional phenomena may be treated as intrinsically real in a limited, conventional sense, while ultimate analysis finds them empty. In Prāsaṅgika, Candrakīrti rejects intrinsic reality at both levels. Conventional phenomena are dependently arisen and causally effective precisely because they lack intrinsic nature; ultimate truth is emptiness, but emptiness is not itself an intrinsic foundation. The source presents these as major philosophical disagreements rather than as one settled Buddhist doctrine.
key_ideas: The two-truths distinction developed over time and may have begun as a useful interpretive device for handling different kinds of Buddhist statements.
Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka theories disagree about what is ultimately real and about how cognition reaches its objects.
Sarvāstivāda identifies ultimate reality with irreducible spatial and temporal units, while wholes and continua are conventionally real.
Sautrāntika identifies ultimate reality with momentary, causally effective unique particulars and treats universals as conceptual constructions.
Yogācāra denies even conventional reality to independently existing physical objects, interpreting experience in terms of mental representations and underlying impressions.

Madhyamaka rejects foundationalism: conventional phenomena dependently arise, and ultimate analysis finds them empty of intrinsic nature; some Madhyamaka thinkers also insist that emptiness is itself empty.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it connects theories of reality and knowledge with Buddhist liberation. It asks what makes an object real, how perception and concepts relate to the world, and whether causal action requires permanent foundations. It also shows why “empty” should not be confused with “nonexistent”: for Madhyamaka, dependence explains ordinary functioning, while analysis blocks the reification of things, selves, and even philosophical conclusions into fixed essences.

important_terms.definition: Truth or reality as established within ordinary linguistic, conceptual, and practical activity; its meaning varies among Buddhist schools.
Truth or reality as disclosed by deeper analysis; different schools identify it with different objects, such as irreducible particulars, mind, or emptiness.
Intrinsic nature or self-existing essence; Madhyamaka arguments deny that phenomena possess this kind of reality.
The absence of intrinsic nature. In Madhyamaka, emptiness is linked to dependent arising rather than to sheer nothingness.
The arising of phenomena through dependence on causes and conditions, a central idea in Madhyamaka explanations of emptiness.
A philosophical view that treats general properties or universals as conceptual constructions rather than independently existing entities.
The five groups used in Buddhist analysis of experience: matter, feeling, perception, dispositions, and consciousness.
A Buddhist goal described in the source as freedom from suffering conditioned by desire and affliction.

questions_to_think_about: If a thing is causally effective, must it possess an intrinsic nature, or could dependence explain its effectiveness?
How does the Yogācāra challenge to external objects differ from the Sautrāntika account of perception?
Why does Madhyamaka reject the idea that emptiness is a final substance beneath ordinary things?
Does the conventional self remain meaningful if analysis finds no independently existing self?
Are disagreements between Svātantrika and Prāsaṅgika merely methodological, or do they involve different views about reality and knowledge?

summaries.example: Suppose your class has a team project. In everyday speech, we say “the team finished the project.” That statement is useful, but the team depends on individual students, their tasks, and the rules that organize them. One philosophical school might say the team is only conventionally real because it can be explained through its parts. A Madhyamaka thinker would also ask whether the students, tasks, or even the smallest parts have an independent essence. The answer would be that they function, but only through dependence.
summaries.summary: Indian Buddhist philosophers developed a theory of two truths: conventional truth concerns ordinary ways of talking and understanding, while ultimate truth concerns deeper analysis. The important point is that there was no single interpretation. Sarvāstivāda thinkers held that everyday objects such as pots are made up of parts and are therefore only conventionally real. They treated atoms and brief moments of consciousness as ultimately real. Sautrāntika philosophers also emphasized momentary particulars, but explained them through direct perception and causal power; general ideas such as universals were, for them, conceptual constructions. Yogācāra philosophers challenged the idea that external physical objects are even conventionally real. They argued that experience consists of mental representations produced by impressions in consciousness. Madhyamaka philosophers criticized all attempts to find a final foundation. Their key claim is that things are empty of intrinsic nature. This does not mean that nothing exists. Rather, things arise dependently and work within ordinary life because of causes, conditions, language, and relations. The source also describes disagreements within Madhyamaka about whether conventional things can be called intrinsically real and about which reasoning methods best reveal emptiness.
key_ideas: The two truths framework became a major way for Buddhist philosophers to interpret teachings and explain reality.
The schools disagreed sharply: some defended physical atoms, some defended momentary particulars, some emphasized mind, and Madhyamaka rejected any final foundation.
For Sarvāstivāda, ordinary wholes are reducible, while atoms and momentary consciousnesses are irreducible.
For Sautrāntika, directly perceived momentary particulars are ultimately real, while general ideas are conventional and concept-dependent.
For Yogācāra, what we experience conventionally is mental representation; independently existing external objects are rejected.
Madhyamaka links conventional truth with dependent arising and ultimate truth with emptiness, while warning that emptiness is not a permanent thing.
summaries.why_it_matters: The two-truths debate matters because it connects abstract questions to how people understand experience, identity, language, and suffering. It shows that “real” can mean different things in different philosophical arguments. It also explains why some Buddhist thinkers thought that seeing dependence and emptiness could support liberation: it loosens the belief that things, including the self, are fixed and independent.

important_terms.definition: What is true or real within ordinary language, concepts, and practical life; it is not interpreted identically by every Buddhist school.
What is found through deeper philosophical or meditative analysis rather than ordinary assumptions.
An independent, permanent essence that would make a thing what it is by itself.
The lack of an independent essence; in Madhyamaka, this is connected with dependence and causal functioning.
The view that general categories, such as “fire” or “team,” are made through concepts rather than existing independently outside thought.
The process by which things arise through causes, conditions, relationships, and dependence.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher distinguish a useful everyday object from the parts that make it up?
What is the difference between directly perceiving one particular event and thinking about a general category?
If all things depend on causes and conditions, does that make them less real or real in a different way?
Why would Yogācāra use dreams or illusions when discussing experience?
How might the idea of an empty self affect ideas about responsibility and change?
